newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM Hashimoto's panel calls for spending cuts.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM Hashimoto's panel calls for spending cuts.

text.p: A Japanese government panel headed by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto released a report on Monday seeking drastic cuts in government spending, in another sign of Hashimoto's drive to improve Japan's debt-ridden finances.
The report called for spending cuts in many areas, in order to keep next year's general expenditures below this year's levels. The next fiscal year begins on April 1, 1998.
Hashimoto has set fiscal reform as one of his top policy goals and has pledged to slash the government deficit to three percent or less of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2003.
Japan's fiscal deficit for calendar 1997 is forecast at about 6.3 percent of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels among major industrialised countries.
The panel was set up in January on Hashimoto's orders and is comprised of government ministers and key ruling party officials.

But Monday's interim report did not mention specific numerical targets for spending cuts, leaving that task open for further discussion. The panel plans to establish targets in its final report by the end of this month.
The interim report called for cuts in the following areas:
- Public works. Annual spending should be decreased by extending the length of a five-year public spending plan while keeping the total amount of spending on the plan unchanged.
- Defense spending. Spending alloted to a five-year plan should be cut.
- Overseas aid. Medium-term targets for Official Development Assistance (ODA) should be abolished.

- Agriculture. Assistance to farmers faced with competition from imports as a result of the Uruguay Round agreement of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade should be scaled back. This should be achieved by extending the period of a six-year assistance plan while keeping the total amount of assistance unchanged.
- Social welfare. Growth in medical costs should be held to the same rate as GDP growth by carrying out structural reforms in the next fiscal year.

The government plans to incorporate the panel's final report into its fiscal reform law, which it aims to submit to an extraordinary session of parliament that is expected to convene in the autumn. -- Tokyo Policy Desk +81-3-5473-3710
